context: For each node in a binary search tree, every value in its left subtree must be smaller than its own and every value in its right subtree must be larger. The arrows point from parent to child.
description: The left diagram, labeled “Balanced binary search tree,” has root 4 with left child 2 and right child 6. Node 2 has left child 1 and right child 3, and 6 has left child 5 and right child 7. The tree has three levels and a height of 2 edges. The right diagram, labeled “Degenerate binary search tree,” has root 7. Following left child pointers gives the chain 7 → 6 → 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. Every right child is empty. The tree has seven levels and a height of 6 edges.

frames.explanation: Both trees contain exactly the values 1 through 7 and strictly satisfy the binary search tree ordering: smaller on the left, larger on the right. Trace a search for leaf 1. The left tree needs only three comparisons along 4 → 2 → 1. The right tree must compare all seven nodes along 7 → 6 → 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. The figure compares two fixed structures. It does not show a sequence of insertions or deletions turning one into the other.
frames.title: Balanced and chain-shaped binary search trees

result: When a binary search tree stays balanced, search, insertion, and deletion take logarithmic time. If it degenerates into a one-sided chain, the worst case visits every node and takes O(n) time.
summary: Two trees with the same seven nodes can both satisfy the search ordering yet have different search path lengths because of their shapes.
title: Balanced and chain-shaped binary search trees
